title: GPU Node Autoscaling and Eviction Playbook for Mixed Workloads
author: Asha Patel
summary: A prescriptive playbook for autoscaling GPU-backed node pools and deterministic eviction behavior under mixed latency and throughput workloads. Covers policy goals, scaling algorithms, eviction heuristics, interactions with preemption and cache-affinity, observability signals, and step-by-step operational procedures for safe rollouts.
body:
Overview:

This playbook describes Redwood's recommended approach to autoscaling GPU node pools and deterministic eviction for mixed inference workloads (latency-sensitive streaming and high-throughput batch requests). The guidance balances cost, latency SLOs, tenant fairness, and model-serving cache affinity. It codifies: scaling triggers, node-granularity decisions, eviction ordering, interaction with GPU preemption and reserved capacity, and monitoring/alerting recipes.

Goals:
- Maintain 99th percentile tail latency SLOs for latency-sensitive routes while minimizing excess idle capacity.
- Ensure predictable eviction and fallback behavior for long-running or large-sequence requests.
- Protect dedicated/reserved capacity and SLA customers from noisy neighbors.
- Preserve KV/prefix cache affinity where feasible to reduce token cost and latency.

Scope and Applicability:
- Applies to all hosted and dedicated GPU pools managed by the cluster autoscaler and Redwood node manager.
- Does NOT replace cloud provider preemption semantics; instead it layers eviction ordering and signaling above cloud APIs.
- Excludes CPU-only pools and offline batch-only clusters (those should follow batch-dedicated scaling guides).

Principles:
1. Latency SLOs trump cost when a request is marked latency-sensitive.
2. Evictions should be deterministic and observable: prefer pre-declared eviction buckets over arbitrary kill orders.
3. Keep common-model and hot-cache workloads on stable nodes; prefer warm node allocation for frequent small requests.
4. Prefer node-level scaling to pod-level autoscaling for GPU allocation stability (one pod per GPU where practical).

Key Concepts and Signals:
- Prometheus metrics referenced: redwood_inference_gpu_utilization, redwood_inference_queue_depth, redwood_inference_request_type_total{route}, redwood_inference_kv_cache_hit_ratio, queue_latency_p50/p90/p99 per route.
- Eviction buckets (higher = more protected): reserved, latency_sensitive, balanced, best_effort.
- Node health signals: CUDANodeTempC, node_gpu_memory_pressure, pod_backoff_count.

Scaling policy (high level):
1. Reactive scale-up: when cluster-global GPU utilization > 75% AND per-pool queue_latency_p90 > 0.75 * route_SLO for > 30s, add node (min 1 node, burst max +3 nodes within 60s).
2. Proactive scale-up: scheduled scale based on forecasted traffic (Horizon: 15–60min) using short-term model from telemetry.
3. Scale-down: only consider nodes with zero active requests and kv_cache_hit_ratio < 10% AND node_gpu_utilization < 25% for > 5 minutes. Stagger scale-down to avoid mass cache loss (max 1 node per pool per 180s).

Suggested autoscaler configuration table (example):
| parameter | recommended value | rationale |
|---|---:|---|
| target_gpu_utilization | 60% | Headroom for tail latency spikes |
| max_burst_nodes | 3 | Allow fast short-term burst for sudden spikes |
| scale_up_cooldown | 20s | Short for rapid reaction to overloads |
| scale_down_cooldown | 300s | Prevent flapping and cache churn |
| min_replicas_per_pool | 2 | Ensure redundancy and reduce noisy neighbor risk |

Eviction policy (deterministic ordering):
1. Mark pods with eviction_score = base_score + tenant_penalty + request_type_penalty + cache_affinity_bonus - grace_bonus.
2. Sort ascending; evict lowest-scored pods first.
3. Eviction scoring components (strings below are metric tags, treat as integers):
   - base_score: 100 for all normal pods
   - tenant_penalty: +0 for reserved tenants, +40 for enterprise, +60 for free-tier
   - request_type_penalty: +0 for latency_sensitive routes, +30 for balanced, +60 for best_effort
   - cache_affinity_bonus: -30 if kv_cache_hit_ratio > 40% on node for that model family
   - grace_bonus: -50 if pod is currently streaming and has held a connection for < 15s (favor draining over immediate kill)

Eviction examples and YAML snippet (Kubernetes Pseudocode):

# Pod annotation to indicate eviction bucket and protection level
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: inference-pod-abc
  annotations:
    inference.redwood.ai/eviction-bucket: "latency_sensitive"
    inference.redwood.ai/tenant-tier: "enterprise"
spec:
  containers:
  - name: runtime
    image: ghcr.io/redwood/runtime:stable

Operational note: The node manager evaluates eviction_score periodically and emits events: NodeManager.EvictionScoreComputed and NodeManager.EvictionCandidateSelected. Use these events for audits.

Interaction with Cloud Preemption and Reserved Capacity:
- If cloud provider signals imminent preemption (e.g., GCP preemption notice), Node Manager attempts graceful drain of non-latency pods and marks reserved pool nodes as protected for 120s.
- Reserved/Dedicated pools set tenant_penalty = -200 to make accidental eviction extremely unlikely.
- For spot/preemptible node pools, scale-down cooldowns are shortened but eviction_score still respected; communicate to scheduler that backup routing to fallback model variants must be enabled.

KV/Prefix Cache Affinity Rules:
- When evicting a node with a hot cache (kv_cache_hit_ratio > 40%), prefer evicting pods whose models do not appear in node cache.
- For batch jobs with large sequence lengths, avoid packing with small latency-sensitive pods on the same node if model families overlap and would thrash GPU memory.

Rolling changes and safe rollout steps:
1. Stage in a canary pool (min 2 nodes) with new autoscaler/eviction logic.
2. Run chaos test: simulate 3x traffic spike and one node preemption; expect no more than 1% SLO violation and no more than 2 node recovers within 120s.
3. Observe metrics for 48h in canary before expanding to 20% of pools.
4. Full rollout: increase incrementally by 20% every 6h, monitor queue_latency_p99, gpu_utilization, and eviction_event_rate.

Testing recipes (automated):
- Load test scenario A: 95% small streaming requests (seq_len < 128) across 5 routes. Verify tail latency stays below SLO during scale-up.
- Load test scenario B: 60% batch long sequences (seq_len > 1024) + 40% streaming. Verify eviction order preserves latency-sensitive pods.
- Chaotic preemption: send simulated preemption notices to 30% of nodes and assert fallback routing triggers and no customer-impacting errors for reserved tenants.

Runbook: What to do if you see mass evictions or cache thinning
1. Pager triggers: queue_latency_p99 > 2x SLO for > 10m OR eviction_event_rate > 5/min for > 5m.
2. Immediate steps:
   a. Escalate to Node Manager oncall, post incident channel, include pool id and recent scale events.
   b. If eviction storms are due to scale-down, temporarily increase min_replicas_per_pool to current node count and disable scale-down for 10 minutes: 
      kubectl annotate nodepool/<POOL> autoscaler.redwood.ai/disable-scale-down=true --overwrite
   c. If preemption notices are present, set fallback routing to max and notify Dedicated customer success for reserved tenants.
3. Recovery steps:
   a. Rehydrate cache by prewarming critical model families: run the prewarm job template (CLI example below).
   b. Re-enable scale-down only after kv_cache_hit_ratio > 25% for 2 consecutive minutes.

Prewarm CLI example:
redwoodctl prewarm --pool <POOL> --model-family llama-2-13b --workers 4 --duration 90s

Monitoring and alerting (recommended dashboards and alerts):
- Dashboards: GPU Pool Overview, Eviction Heatmap (per-pool), Cache Affinity Map, Tail Latency by Route.
- Alert rules (examples):
  - Alert: EvictionStormHigh
    expr: increase(node_manager_eviction_events_total[5m]) > 20
    severity: page
  - Alert: LatencySLOBreachCandidate
    expr: queue_latency_p99 / route_slo > 1.5
    severity: page
  - Alert: HotCacheLoss
    expr: avg_over_time(redwood_inference_kv_cache_hit_ratio[5m]) < 0.15 and node_count_scaling_events > 3
    severity: ticket

Ownership and Escalation:
- Primary owner: infra-scheduling team (oncall alias infra-scheduling@redwood.ai)
- Secondary owner: serving-runtime team (oncall alias serving-runtime@redwood.ai)
- When reserved/dedicated tenant impact is suspected, notify customer-success-enterprise immediately.

Related pages and references:
- See: architecture-and-standards/infra-standards/gpu-thermal-power-aware-scheduling-standards-2025.json (thermal interaction patterns)
- See: eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/sequence-length-aware-kernel-selection-guidelines-2026.json (kernel selection rules)

Appendix: Quick reference thresholds (copyable)
- scale_up_trigger_utilization: 0.75
- scale_down_max_idle_time_secs: 300
- node_protection_duration_on_preemption_notice_secs: 120
- hot_cache_hit_ratio_threshold: 0.40
